what_its_for: Lanreotide is used to treat acromegaly (a condition where the body makes too much growth hormone), as well as certain tumors of the stomach, intestines, or pancreas called neuroendocrine tumors (NETs). It works by slowing down the release of certain hormones in your body.
how_to_take: Lanreotide is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in the upper outer part of your buttock. Your doctor, nurse, or trained caregiver will give you this injection. After proper training, you or a caregiver may be able to give the injection at home. The medication comes in a pre-filled syringe that is ready to use. Do not shake the syringe. Rotate injection sites to avoid skin irritation at the same spot.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 90 mg given once every 4 weeks (once a month). Your doctor may adjust your dose to 60 mg or 120 mg once every 4 weeks depending on how well your condition is controlled and how you respond to treatment. In some stable patients, your doctor may space out injections to once every 6 or 8 weeks. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled injection appointment, contact your doctor or healthcare provider as soon as possible to reschedule. Try to stay on your regular monthly schedule. Do not try to make up for a missed dose by giving two injections at once. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist right away.
storage: Store lanreotide in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in the original box and protect it from light until you are ready to use it. Do not freeze lanreotide. If needed, it can be kept at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for a short period. Keep this medication out of reach of children. Do not use it if the expiration date on the package has passed.
what_to_avoid: Avoid alcohol, as it may worsen certain side effects like dizziness or stomach upset. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, as lanreotide can interact with medicines for diabetes, heart rhythm problems, and cyclosporine. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or tired after your injection. Do not skip follow-up appointments, as regular blood tests and imaging are important to monitor your treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe stomach pain, nausea, or vomiting (possible signs of gallstones or pancreatitis); unusual changes in your blood sugar (signs of high blood sugar include increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurry vision; signs of low blood sugar include shakiness, sweating, or confusion); slow or irregular heartbeat; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; significant pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site; or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Lanreotide begins working shortly after your first injection, but it may take several weeks to months before you notice the full benefits, such as reduced symptoms or lower hormone levels. Your doctor will check your hormone levels and symptoms regularly with blood tests and possibly imaging scans to see how well the medication is working for you. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor, even if you feel better.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): Lanreotide can generally be used safely in older patients, but your doctor will monitor you more closely for side effects such as gallstones or blood sugar changes. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more carefully if you have severe kidney or liver disease. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Lanreotide may harm an unborn baby, and it is not known if it passes into breast milk. Your doctor will discuss the risks and benefits with you. Children: The safety and effectiveness of lanreotide in children have not been fully established. Use in children is determined on a case-by-case basis by your doctor.
